provenance.source_title: The water footprint of artificial intelligence: Emerging solutions and governance imperatives

reading_path.moves: Frames the subject as both a technical problem and a governance imperative; previews quantitative, institutional, and normative claims.

claims.text: AI's global water footprint could reach 4.2–6.6 billion cubic meters by 2027.

evidence.text: AI's global water footprint could reach 4.2–6.6 billion cubic meters by 2027.

claims.text: Two-thirds of post-2022 data centers are located in water-stressed regions.

evidence.text: Two-thirds of post-2022 data centers are located in water-stressed regions.

claims.text: Technical solutions exist, but policy gaps limit their deployment.

evidence.text: Technical solutions exist but deployment remains limited by policy gaps.

claims.text: Digital water sobriety links AI evaluation to water constraints, and water-sustainable AI requires mandatory facility-level transparency.

evidence.text: Digital water sobriety framework links AI evaluation to water constraints.
Mandatory facility-level transparency needed for water-sustainable AI.

reading_path.meaning: The opening presents water use as something requiring public direction, not merely improved engineering. These are initial propositions rather than conclusions established at this point in the reading.

reading_path.moves: Maps the system boundary, identifies a neglected environmental dimension, introduces a framework, and states the article's thesis.

claims.text: AI increasingly uses high-density computing infrastructure, but environmental assessment still concentrates mainly on electricity and greenhouse-gas emissions.

evidence.text: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly run on high-density computing infrastructure, yet its environmental footprint is still assessed mainly through electricity use and associated greenhouse-gas emissions.

claims.text: AI infrastructure uses freshwater through evaporative cooling, electricity generation, and semiconductor manufacturing.

evidence.text: AI infrastructure consumes freshwater through evaporative cooling, indirect water use in electricity generation, and water-intensive semiconductor manufacturing.
The diagram connects AI expansion to data centers and then to three water-use pathways, with separate branches for technical solutions and policy responses.

claims.text: Digital water sobriety combines evaluation of which AI applications justify freshwater use, water-conscious siting, and mandatory facility-level transparency.

evidence.text: This work introduces "digital water sobriety" as a governance framework linking evaluation of which AI applications justify freshwater consumption, water conscious siting, and mandatory facility-level water use transparency.

claims.text: Water-sustainable AI demands fundamental policy reform integrating water constraints into infrastructure planning, not merely technological optimization.

evidence.text: Achieving water-sustainable AI demands not merely technological optimization but fundamental policy reform integrating water constraints into computational infrastructure planning.

reading_path.meaning: The abstract expands the opening highlights into a causal map and an explicit policy thesis. It also establishes that the value of AI applications themselves, rather than only their efficiency, belongs within the proposed discussion.

reading_path.moves: Contrasts user experience with material infrastructure; introduces illustrative estimates and conditional projections.

claims.text: AI appears intangible and effectively costless to users, while each conversation, generated image, and training run produces waste heat that often requires water-intensive cooling.

evidence.text: The introduction contrasts the largely invisible water and energy footprint with the waste heat produced at distant data centers by every AI conversation, image generation, and model-training run; that heat often must be removed through water-intensive cooling.

claims.text: Training GPT-3 required approximately 700,000 liters of clean freshwater, and generating 10–50 medium-length responses consumes the equivalent of a 500 ml bottle.

evidence.text: recent analysis by Li et al. (2024) estimated that training GPT-3 required approximately 700,000 liters of clean freshwater, while generating 10–50 medium-length responses consumes the equivalent of a 500 ml water bottle.

citations.reference_entry: Li, X., Ren, S., Arlington, U., 2024. Addressing the water footprint of artificial intelligence: a path towards sustainability. arXiv preprint arXiv: 2304.03271v5..

claims.text: If increasing AI use continues, AI's global annual water footprint could reach 4.2–6.6 billion cubic meters by 2027, while U.S. data centers alone are projected to consume up to 280 billion liters annually by 2028.

evidence.text: The introduction presents the global projection conditionally on continued growth in AI use and places it alongside the U.S. data-center projection.

reading_path.meaning: The introduction makes the hidden infrastructure tangible through a model-training example, an everyday bottle comparison, and growth projections. It has not yet explained how different kinds of water accounting relate to these figures.

reading_path.location: Page 2, Section 1, footprint components and scope
reading_path.moves: Disaggregates the footprint and narrows the review's scope.

claims.text: AI's water footprint has three interconnected components: direct cooling and humidification, indirect electricity-generation water use, and water embedded in semiconductor manufacturing.

evidence.text: The source enumerates these three components and reports that chip fabrication consumes thousands of liters per wafer.

citations.reference_entry: Yañez-Barnuevo, M., 2025. Data centers and water consumption. https://www.eesi.org/articles/view/data-centers-and-water-consumption (accessed 07.12.25).

claims.text: Operational cooling water consumption is the most substantial and directly manageable portion, and is therefore the focus of this work.

evidence.text: This work focuses on operational water consumption for cooling, as it constitutes the most substantial and directly manageable portion.

reading_path.meaning: The article moves from an expansive footprint concept to a deliberately narrower operational focus. The scope is justified both by claimed magnitude and by manageability.

reading_path.moves: Compares AI with conventional cloud computing, supplies mechanisms and figures, and draws a conclusion about the need for dedicated assessment.

claims.text: All data centers consume water for cooling, but AI workloads intensify demand beyond traditional cloud computing through greater computational power, electricity use, and heat generation.

evidence.text: The first distinguishing characteristic links accelerated servers' computational demands to higher electricity consumption, greater heat generation, and advanced cooling requirements.

claims.text: AI training runs maintain near-100% GPU utilization for weeks or months, eliminating cooling downtime and maximizing cumulative water consumption over training periods.

evidence.text: Unlike transactional workloads with variable load patterns that allow cooling systems to modulate operation, AI training runs operate at near-100% GPU utilization continuously for weeks or months. This eliminates opportunities for cooling system downtime and maximizes cumulative water consumption over training periods.

claims.text: Hyperscale AI facilities concentrate water demand and amplify local stress; their rack power densities are 50–100+ kW compared with 5–10 kW in conventional enterprise facilities.

evidence.text: The source says one hyperscale AI training site can concentrate demand equivalent to dozens of smaller conventional data centers and supplies the contrasting rack-power-density ranges.

claims.text: AI infrastructure poses a qualitatively different water challenge from general-purpose cloud computing and warrants dedicated assessment and mitigation strategies.

evidence.text: These distinctions establish that AI infrastructure presents a qualitatively different water challenge from general-purpose cloud computing, warranting dedicated assessment and mitigation strategies.

reading_path.meaning: The argument now explains why AI is being treated separately from data centers generally. Its conclusion rests on intensity, duration, and spatial concentration rather than simply on the presence of cooling.

reading_path.moves: Describes evidence selection and establishes a source hierarchy.

claims.text: The review synthesizes three evidence streams: peer-reviewed studies, corporate reports and technical documentation, and investigative journalism and policy analyses.

evidence.text: The targeted review used Web of Science and Google Scholar for 2015–2025 studies, prioritizing quantitative assessments and lifecycle analyses; reports from Google, Microsoft, and AWS; and journalism and policy analyses on siting, regulation, and community impacts.

claims.text: Peer-reviewed sources were prioritized over corporate documentation and journalism or policy analysis.

evidence.text: Peer-reviewed sources were prioritized over the other two sources.

reading_path.meaning: The discussion pauses to explain how its evidence was assembled. It identifies a targeted synthesis rather than presenting an original measurement study or a fully specified systematic-review protocol.

reading_path.moves: Defines accounting categories and distinguishes environmental mechanisms.

claims.text: Water footprint is a broad framework for freshwater appropriation, formally standardized in ISO 14046, distinguishing blue, green, and grey water.

evidence.text: The source defines blue water as surface and groundwater consumption, green water as rainwater stored in soil, and grey water as the volume needed to assimilate pollutants.

evidence.text: The source says it synthesizes quantitative data as reported in literature and corporate disclosures, and identifies the broader assessment as a research priority.

reading_path.meaning: The author explicitly separates the desired focus on consumption from the less cleanly differentiated available data. This qualification remains relevant whenever later passages use reported water volumes.

claims.text: Transparency remains severely limited because operators frequently withhold facility-level data as commercially sensitive, preventing reliable footprint assessment.

evidence.text: Yet transparency remains severely limited. Operators frequently withhold facility-level data as commercially sensitive, preventing reliable assessment of AI's water footprint.

claims.text: Comprehensive understanding requires facility locations, cooling configurations, and electricity sources, which remain missing or aggregated.

evidence.text: The passage identifies these three categories as required disclosures.

citations.reference_entry: Jain, P., 2025. From bottleneck to breakthrough: AI in chip verification: how AI is transforming chip design with smarter verification methods. https://spectrum.ieee.org/calibre-vision-ai-chip-design (accessed 05.12.25).

claims.text: Standardized reporting protocols and mandatory disclosure are critical priorities for quantifying AI's true water impact and enabling evidence-based governance.

evidence.text: Developing standardized reporting protocols and mandatory disclosure requirements are critical priorities for quantifying AI's true water impact and enabling evidence-based governance.

reading_path.meaning: The disclosure demand becomes more operational: WUE alone is not the whole requested record. Location, cooling design, and electricity sources are needed to connect reported volumes to local and indirect effects.

reading_path.location: Pages 5–6, Section 6 opening and Section 6.1, AI-specific accounting
reading_path.moves: Restates feasibility, opens a research agenda, and identifies workload attribution as a bottleneck.

claims.text: Critical knowledge gaps and implementation barriers remain despite the demonstrated feasibility of water-efficient AI through technology and policy.

evidence.text: Section 6 repeats that water-efficient AI is achievable through innovation and intervention, then introduces five interconnected research priorities as major bottlenecks.

claims.text: Current accounting measures facility consumption without attributing water costs to particular models, training runs, or architectural choices.

evidence.text: Current methodologies measure facility-level consumption without attributing water costs to specific models, training runs, or architectural choices.

claims.text: Benchmarks linking workloads to water consumption across cooling configurations would support targeted optimization and application-level judgments about justified use in stressed watersheds.

evidence.text: Benchmark datasets linking workload characteristics to water consumption across cooling configurations would enable targeted optimization and inform application-level decisions about which AI deployments justify their water costs in stressed watersheds.

reading_path.meaning: The research agenda exposes a measurement requirement of the sobriety framework: judging applications requires finer attribution than facility totals presently provide.

reading_path.location: Page 6, Section 6.1, lifecycle integration and ecological monitoring
reading_path.moves: Identifies missing indirect accounting, recommends spatiotemporal lifecycle methods, and returns to unresolved aquatic effects.

claims.text: Indirect water in electricity and semiconductor manufacturing remains poorly quantified, especially as grids move toward renewables with different water intensities.

evidence.text: Indirect water embedded in electricity generation and semiconductor manufacturing remains poorly quantified, particularly as grids shift toward renewables with different water intensities.

claims.text: Integrated lifecycle assessment should incorporate spatial and temporal variation in regional electricity-generation profiles, as agricultural accounting does.

evidence.text: The recommendation invokes agricultural work as an example of spatially and temporally differentiated accounting.

citations.reference_entry: Pfister, S., Bayer, P., 2014. Monthly water stress: spatially and temporally explicit consumptive water footprint of global crop production. J. Clean Prod. 73, 52–62.

claims.text: Ecological monitoring is a research priority because lakeside and subsea approaches can minimize consumption while altering thermal regimes.

evidence.text: The Ecological impact monitoring item restates possible effects of approximately 5–8 °C discharge warming on stratification, dissolved oxygen, and aquatic ecosystems.

reading_path.meaning: Earlier scope exclusions become explicit research tasks. The ecological item repeats the thermal concern as a reason to collect evidence, maintaining the distinction between reducing consumed volume and establishing overall environmental benefit.

reading_path.location: Page 6, Section 6.1, district heating and disclosure protocols
reading_path.moves: Identifies comparative economic evidence gaps and specifies requirements for standardized measurement.

claims.text: Although pilots demonstrate district-heating viability, cross-city evidence on costs, legacy-network integration, and use under different conditions remains limited.

evidence.text: While pilot projects demonstrate technical viability, cross-city evidence on costs, integration with legacy networks, and usage under different conditions remains limited.

claims.text: Inconsistent voluntary reporting prevents meaningful comparisons and evidence-based policy; standardized measurement methods, temporal resolution, and geographical granularity are foundational to governance and watershed assessment.

evidence.text: The Standardized disclosure protocols item states both the limitation of current reporting and the required dimensions of a common protocol.

reading_path.meaning: The agenda closes by pairing technical-economic comparability with reporting comparability. Both are treated as enabling conditions for practical governance, not simply as additional descriptive research.

reading_path.moves: Consolidates policy recommendations and adds concrete scope to disclosure and permitting.

claims.text: Mandatory facility-level WUE reporting should cover on-site consumption, water embedded in electricity, and temporal variation to enable watershed-level assessment.

evidence.text: Extending WUE reporting requirements to include on-site consumption, embedded water in electricity supply, and temporal variation would enable watershed-level assessment.

claims.text: New construction should be restricted in severely stressed watersheds, and concessions and permits should require cumulative-impact assessment to avoid externalizing costs onto vulnerable communities.

evidence.text: Restrict new construction in severely-stressed watersheds and require cumulative impact assessment as part of water concession and permitting processes, to avoid externalizing costs onto vulnerable communities.

reading_path.meaning: The recommendations become more directive than the earlier list of possible instruments. In particular, siting policy now includes an explicit restriction on new construction in severely stressed watersheds.

reading_path.location: Page 6, Section 6.2, sobriety frameworks and heat-recovery incentives
reading_path.moves: Restates the framework as a policy imperative and recommends system-integration incentives.

claims.text: Tiered governance should link AI deployment to demonstrated societal benefit and local water availability rather than computational economics alone.

evidence.text: The Digital water sobriety frameworks item calls for tiered governance and repeats scarcity-adjusted pricing, large-training water assessments, facility budgets, and preferential permitting, while explicitly contrasting resource constraints with computational economics alone.
evidence.locator: Page 6, Section 6.2, Digital water sobriety frameworks

claims.text: Policies favoring district-heating integration over simpler direct cooling would accelerate system-level solutions that displace fossil thermal generation and associated water use, providing energy, climate, and water co-benefits.

evidence.text: Policy frameworks incentivizing district heating integration over simpler direct cooling approaches would accelerate deployment of system-level solutions that displace fossil thermal generation and associated water use, delivering co-benefits across energy, climate, and water domains.
evidence.locator: Page 6, Section 6.2, Heat recovery integration incentives

reading_path.meaning: The section gathers earlier proposals into a coherent program. The heat-recovery recommendation also returns to the broader energy system, preserving the article's concern that facility-only metrics miss consequential effects.

reading_path.moves: Reframes the central issue, reuses contrasting examples, and draws a strong attribution of responsibility.

claims.text: As energy and freshwater become constrained, the central issue shifts from marginal efficiency to resource justice: how much intelligence per liter is justified.

evidence.text: As AI expands, the central question shifts from marginal efficiency to resource justice: how much "intelligence" per liter of water is justified as both energy and freshwater become constrained?

claims.text: Luleå's roughly 25 million liters annually and China's zero-freshwater subsea installations suggest that outcomes reflect policy and siting choices rather than technological necessity.

evidence.text: Technical pathways exist: Meta's Luleå facility demonstrates 25 million liters annually suffices for hyperscale operations, while China's subsea installations achieve zero freshwater consumption, suggesting outcomes reflect policy and siting choices, not technological necessity.

claims.text: Colón epitomizes governance failures in siting, disclosure, and treating water as unlimited; public-water consumption by computational infrastructure during drought while agricultural communities face restrictions is a governance failure, not a technical constraint.

evidence.text: The conclusion names electricity-cost-prioritizing siting, obscured local impacts, and frameworks treating water as unlimited, then explicitly calls the contrast between industrial consumption and agricultural restrictions a governance failure rather than a technical constraint.
evidence.locator: Page 6, Section 6.3, second paragraph continuing into right column

reading_path.meaning: The conclusion returns to the same examples but gives them a more explicit role in assigning responsibility. Efficiency remains relevant, yet the governing question has become whose claims on a shared resource take priority.

reading_path.moves: Presents alternative futures, emphasizes institutional timing, and ends with an urgent political challenge.

claims.text: Choices about deployment, cooling, and whose water is consumed will determine whether AI worsens water insecurity for vulnerable populations or stimulates integrated water-energy-heat innovation.

evidence.text: The choices made regarding where AI is deployed, how it is cooled, and whose water it consumes will determine whether this technology exacerbates water insecurity for vulnerable populations or catalyzes innovation in integrated water-energy-heat systems.

claims.text: Whether governance, corporate accountability, and public awareness develop fast enough to redirect current trajectories will shape both AI's future and the equity and sustainability of shared water resources.

evidence.text: Whether governance structures, corporate accountability mechanisms, and public awareness develop rapidly enough to redirect current trajectories will shape not only AI's technological future but the equity and sustainability of our shared hydrological resources.

claims.text: Water-sustainable AI is achievable; the question is whether society has the political will to implement it before computational expansion irreversibly deepens stress in already vulnerable regions.

evidence.text: Water-sustainable AI is achievable, the question is whether the society possesses the political will to implement it before computational expansion irreversibly deepens water stress in already vulnerable regions.

reading_path.meaning: The final passage is not a neutral forecast: it presents a consequential choice and an urgent deadline implied by potentially irreversible worsening. The article ends by locating the decisive obstacle in political will rather than unavailable cooling technology.

reading_path.location: Pages 6–7, authorship statement, competing-interest declaration, data availability, and References
reading_path.moves: Closes with research disclosures and the bibliography supporting the review.

The bibliography completes the record of the mixed scholarly, corporate, journalistic, and policy sources described in the methodology; it does not add a new substantive argument.
